what_it_does: Every time a language model generates a word, the most expensive computation is 'attention'—consulting the model's running notes (the key-value cache, which records context for each user request) stored in GPU memory. Different serving systems store those notes in different layouts (paged tables, prefix trees, etc.) and use different attention variants (grouped heads, sliding windows, custom score modifications), forcing developers to maintain dozens of specialized GPU programs. FlashInfer is a single attention engine that handles all these cases through a unified data format, a just-in-time compiler that generates optimized GPU programs on demand, and a load-balancing scheduler that keeps all GPU cores busy even when requests have very different lengths.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Three separate problems plague attention in production serving: storage heterogeneity (notes are stored in pages, trees, or flat arrays depending on the system), variant diversity (grouped-query attention, sliding windows, custom logit modifications, different normalization schemes), and load imbalance (short and long requests mixed in a batch leave some GPU processing units idle). FlashInfer solves all three with one design.

Unified storage. FlashInfer represents every storage layout—paged tables, radix prefix trees, tree attention for speculative decoding—as a Block Sparse Row (BSR) matrix, a standard data structure that groups non-zero entries into rectangular blocks and stores their positions in an index array. The block size (Br x Bc) is tunable: a large Br lets multiple requests share the same cached prefix in fast GPU shared memory; a small Br handles unique-suffix data through global memory. Requests that share a common prompt prefix use a 'composable format'—two separate BSR matrices, one for the shared prefix (large block, shared memory) and one for the unique suffix (small block)—with partial attention outputs mathematically merged afterward using the log-sum-exp composition identity.

Customizable attention via JIT compilation. Users describe an attention variant by writing a small functor class specifying any custom transformations of queries, keys, values, logits, or outputs. FlashInfer's JIT (just-in-time) compiler slots this functor into a pre-written CUDA GPU-program template and compiles it on first use, caching the result. This means supporting a new attention variant requires roughly 20 lines of code instead of a new fully hand-tuned GPU program.

Load-balanced scheduling. Long key-value sequences are split into chunks and assigned to GPU thread blocks using a priority-queue algorithm inspired by the Stream-K scheduling technique, ensuring all thread blocks finish at roughly the same time regardless of sequence-length variation. The scheduler runs on the CPU between generation steps and writes a plan into GPU memory; the GPU kernel reads the plan and runs persistently with a fixed launch grid, making it compatible with CUDAGraph—a mechanism that replays a pre-recorded sequence of GPU operations, eliminating Python overhead.

The result. Versus Triton-compiled attention kernels in the SGLang serving framework, FlashInfer reduces per-token latency by 29–69%. It cuts long-context inference latency by 28–30% and parallel generation latency by 13–17%.
